posts.author: Kiffdino
posts.content_md:
Over the past year I had some trouble with my laser.

What happened: I have a dongle on my laser unit, on which i can tune the power output by turning a little screw on it eather clockwise or counterclockwise.

There are two lamps on that dongle. 

Lamp1 goes on when I turn the power on.

Lamp2 comes on, when the laser has reached the output power I have set on the dongle and REMAINS stable.

As soon as the laser becomes unstable lamp2 comes off, and stays off until the laser becomes stable again.

Ok all of this is probably not new to most of you.

So Im doing DCG and running this green laser at full power, all the time.

One day I notice the second lamp going off at times, and then it takes about 30 sec until it goes on again.

If this happened during exposure, there was no hologram.

So I asked Sam, what the problem could be, and he was very helpful, even though I didn't buy the laser from him.

He first suspected maybe a cable break or the diode had reached the end of its life time.

So after changing the cable and still getting the problem, I was quitly being mad at Jem i initially baught the laser from for selling me an old unit, because I didn't put that many hours on it.

Today I realized, my anger at him was probably uncalled for.

I noticed in my lab at times, that the entire light would dim for about a split second and the come back up again.

So today in an last effort to figure out why the laser was acting funny I took it out of the lab, braught it home, plugged it and it was running perfect at full power for about 30 min, when I switched it off again.

So my guess is, that someone near my lab is pulling huge amounts of power out of the grid, and that this is somehow effecting me, im suspecting a print shop nearby.

Talking to my landlord or the power company is no option, because of reasons that i dont want to elaborate on right now.

I might need to add, the wiring in my lab is about 70 years old.

**So my question is: Is there an option to run the laser independently of my local power grid.... maybe a battery... or do you think putting something like a Magnetic mains regulator inbetween would solve the problem ?**

posts.author: Johnfp
posts.content_md:
I am not sure of your set up, but most industrial places, at least here in the US, have 3 phase electricity. The compass 315 runs on a single leg and ground. It is very possible that the spike in usage could be from just one or two of those legs from the 3 phase. If you can test all three legs coming into your building, it may be you can piggy back off of of one of the legs that does not get the drop in voltage.

Just a thought.

posts.author: Johnfp
posts.content_md:
If you dont have 3 phase, then you can test the other leg coming into your building to see if it gets a voltage drop also. 

Here is the inside of 220V breaker boxes here in the US. Depending on which breaker you are on will determine which leg you are pulling from. If the other leg has no issue, you can simply switch to a breaker on the other leg (busbar).

[http://waterheatertimer.org/images/Insi ... ox-420.jpg](http://waterheatertimer.org/images/Inside-Main-Breaker-Box-420.jpg)

posts.author: rzeheb
posts.content_md: What about running it off of a UPS (uninterruptable power supply)? We use those in my lab to support vital equipment in the event of an unexpected power loss. Depending on the size of the UPS, they can handle a reasonably high power draw. They are also very good at "conditioning" the power and will suppress power surges as well as supplement power in the event of a reduction in line voltage. Just a thought, but I can't think of any reason why it wouldn't work.

posts.author: John Klayer

I measured it again with the ammeter hardwired into the line:

1.97 Amps @ 25.2 Volts at start (just a few seconds)

.41 to .52 Amps during search

.49 Amps @ 25.3 Volts when both lights lit and stable

So it does want 50 Watts for a few seconds then lives happily with a dozen.
